text_blocks.snippet: Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed by a healthcare provider using specific blood tests that measure your blood sugar or average glucose levels.
snippet_highlighted_words: by a healthcare provider using specific blood tests that measure your blood sugar or average glucose levels

list.snippet: A1C Test: Measures your average blood sugar level over the past 2 to 3 months.
Diabetes range: 6.5% or higher on two separate tests.
Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) Test: Measures your blood sugar after you do not eat or drink anything (except water) for at least 8 hours.
Diabetes range: 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or higher on two separate tests.
Prediabetes range: 100 to 125 mg/dL (5.6 to 6.9 mmol/L).
Random Plasma Glucose Test: Measures your blood sugar at any time of day, regardless of when you last ate.
Diabetes range: 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or higher, if you also have classic symptoms of high blood sugar (such as extreme thirst, frequent urination, fatigue, or blurry vision).
Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT): Measures your blood sugar before and 2 hours after you drink a special sugary liquid.
Diabetes range: 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or higher after 2 hours.
Prediabetes range: 140 to 199 mg/dL (7.8 to 11.0 mmol/L).
Repeat Testing: Except in cases of a random test with clear symptoms, doctors usually confirm a diabetes diagnosis by repeating one of the tests on a different day.

Who Should Get Tested: The American Diabetes Association recommends screening for all adults age 35 or older (or age 45 and older), as well as younger adults who are overweight or have additional risk factors like high blood pressure or a family history of diabetes. You can evaluate your personal risk using the ADA 60-Second Risk Test.
